newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica finance minister focus of race-criticism row.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica finance minister focus of race-criticism row.

text.p: South Africa's ruling ANC condemned critics of black Finance Minister Trevor Manuel on Tuesday as racists, a party strategy that political analysts said was beginning to wear thin.
"The cheapest shot they have is race to silence people," said Joseph Diescho, a political scientist at the University of South Africa.

He and other analysts said the vehemence of the African National Congress reaction to speculation that Manuel might be moved in a cabinet reshuffle could not hide the doubts that existed about his suitability for the job.
"I know many people in the ANC are saying, 'Is he really qualified to have this ministry?'," Diescho said.
"Emotionally, he's fine. But that's a very rational ministry where you need a person who has to be seen more as a technocrat than as an activist or a good ANC cadre, and there people are split...
"When they link his arrival in the ministry with the rapid drop of the rand, they can only feel jittery," Diescho said.
Manuel, appointed in April to replace white former banker Chris Liebenberg, arrived in the job two months after the rand began a dramatic plunge against foreign currencies.
The decline was initially attributed to a range of factors, including unfounded rumours about President Nelson Mandela's health, which no longer seem to apply.
But the currency has remained weak.

Last week newspapers quoted unnamed ANC sources as saying Mandela planned to reshuffle his cabinet next month and that Manuel might make way for a white minister, current Trade and Industry Minister Alec Erwin.
Mandela's spokesman denied the reports on Friday and on Tuesday the ANC issued its own statement calling the speculation "racist, uninformed and unintelligible".

But Diescho noted: "The speculation is not only within the media, it's also within the ANC itself. It has to do with the rationality of having Trevor Manuel as minister of a very rational department."
An authority on the ANC at the University of the Witwatersrand, Professor Tom Lodge, said the party knew very well that newspaper speculation was based on leaks within the ANC.

"The ANC shouldn't start blaming the press but it should also understand that leaks are a normal part of democracy. And unless it wants a monolithic organisation, they are going to continue to happen," he said.
"This sort of outburst from the ANC simply demonstrates inexperience and shouldn't be taken too seriously...it's business as usual."
Lodge said speculation about cabinet reshuffles was a feature of democracies everywhere.
"Speculation about a finance minister who has presided over a 25 percent devaluation of the rand is predictable and need not be directly influenced by racist considerations," he said.
"Shouting race isn't the point. It doesn't matter whether perceptions are racist, what matters is the strength of our currency.
"The people who often influence the way our economy is regarded internationally may well be racist, but we can't do much about that," Lodge said.
He said Manuel had limited experience before taking on the portfolio, so it was unsurprising that markets had been apprehensive.
"On the other hand, I don't think anyone could pinpoint any particular action by him or any decision made by him that could be criticised," Lodge added.
"Crying 'unfair' misses the point. The international capitalist marketplace and particularly that which refers to currencies is an unfair place."
